concept.name: Risk capacity
concept.definition: The maximum loss an individual or organization can financially absorb without jeopardizing essential goals or solvency - what one is able to risk, as opposed to risk tolerance, which is what one is willing to risk. In the ISO-derived framing, capability bounds willingness: the accepted level of risk should never exceed capacity.
concept.intuition: Tolerance is about nerves; capacity is about math - the rent money has no risk capacity no matter how brave you feel.
concept.mechanics: Computed from objective constraints: income stability, time horizon, liquidity needs, leverage, dependents, and obligations. Prudent practice sizes risk to the lesser of capacity and tolerance; exceeding capacity risks ruin regardless of psychological comfort.
concept.failure_modes: Capacity is often misjudged by ignoring correlated obligations (job loss plus drawdown, margin calls plus illiquidity) and it shrinks abruptly in crises exactly when positions are largest. Using tolerance rather than capacity for sizing is a classic path to ruin.
concept.misconceptions: High risk tolerance does not create risk capacity, and neither youth nor confidence substitutes for reserves. Capacity is also dynamic - it changes with wealth, income, and liabilities, so it must be re-estimated.
concept.example: A trader with three months of living expenses saved and a variable income has near-zero capacity for a $10,000 drawdown, whatever his appetite, so per-trade risk must be sized to capacity.
